title: Run a kerosene wick heater safely
summary: A kerosene wick heater can warm a room through a power cut with no electricity at all, if it gets water-clear 1-K kerosene, a wick set to the maker's height and a door open to the rest of the house (and a window cracked if the house is tight) for air. Petrol in the tank, refuelling it hot, or running it in a closed room are what start fires and poison people.

materials.item: Water-clear 1-K kerosene in a blue or clearly marked kerosene can

materials.qty: 1 in the room, 1 where people sleep

materials.item: Spare wick made for this heater's model
Class B or ABC fire extinguisher

steps.text: Check the fuel before anything else. Use only water-clear 1-K kerosene. Reject fuel that is yellow, cloudy, sour-smelling, has a water layer, or came from a red can or any can that ever held petrol or solvent (CPSC 5052, Toyotomi KS-27A).
steps.warn: Even a little petrol mixed into kerosene can make the heater flare out of control or explode (CPSC 5052).

steps.text: Put the heater on a firm, level floor at least 1 m (3 ft) from walls, curtains, bedding, shelves, furniture and clothing, or the label's distance if it is larger (Toyotomi: 90 cm for the KS-27A, 1 m for the Omni 230; MSU E-1669 names bedding), out of draughts, doorways and walkways (Toyotomi KS-27A). Never in a bathroom or a small room with the door shut (Toyotomi KS-27A). Nothing goes on top of it: Toyotomi says it is not a cooking or water-heating appliance, so no kettle or pot (Toyotomi KS-27A). Keep it out of any space with petrol, solvent or paint-thinner vapour, and keep children and pets back, behind a barrier if you can (Toyotomi KS-27A, MSU E-1669).

Set up the air before you light it: keep the room's door open to the rest of the house. If the door must be shut, or the house is tight or weather-stripped, also open an outside window about 2.5 cm (1 in) (CPSC 5052). Put a working CO alarm in the room, not right beside the heater, and one where people sleep. Check its temperature rating and expiry date (safety_carbon_monoxide).
steps.warn: The heater always puts some carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide into the room (CPSC 5052). A closed room lets them build up.

steps.text: Fill it outdoors, only when it is off and cold, with a siphon pump. Stop at the full mark: very cold kerosene swells as it warms indoors and can overflow (Toyotomi KS-27A). Put the cap back tight and wipe up every drip.
steps.warn: Never fill a heater that is burning or still hot: the vapour can flash back to the can (Toyotomi KS-27A).

steps.text: After fitting a new wick, filling the heater for the first time, or refuelling it after it has been out of fuel for a long time, wait about 30 minutes for kerosene to soak up the wick before lighting it. Lighting a dry wick can ruin it (Toyotomi KS-27A).

Burn a brand-new heater for about 15 minutes outside the living space the first time you light it, to burn off the protective oil on the burner parts; it smells if done inside, and Toyotomi says it is needed only that first time (Toyotomi KS-27A). Toyotomi suggests a garage or a spot outdoors out of strong draughts; in a garage, keep the big door open and keep it clear of petrol and solvent fumes (Toyotomi KS-27A, safety_carbon_monoxide).

Light it: raise the wick fully. A model with a battery igniter, like the Omni 230, lights as the knob turns. Otherwise tilt or lift the heat chamber and touch a match to the top of the wick, without leaving the burnt match on it. Then make sure the heat chamber is seated by moving its handle side to side (Toyotomi KS-27A, Toyotomi Omni 230, CPSC 5052).

Set the flame after about 10 minutes, once the chamber is hot. The chamber should glow evenly. Too high gives smoke and soot; too low gives a smell. Never run it below the lowest wick stop (Toyotomi KS-27A, CPSC 5052). Watch it closely for the first 15 to 20 minutes (Toyotomi KS-27A).

Turn it off with the wick knob, all the way down, before you sleep or leave the room. Keep the emergency lever for emergencies: using it or bumping the heater to shut it off makes smoke and smell. Wait at least 3 minutes before relighting (Toyotomi KS-27A).

If flames come out of the heater or it flares up, do not carry it, try to smother it or throw water on it. Use the manual shut-off if it has one; if that does not stop it, get everyone out (CPSC 5052). Only a class B (or ABC) extinguisher suits it (Toyotomi KS-27A).
steps.warn: Flames outside the heater body mean the fuel is contaminated with petrol or something like it (Toyotomi KS-27A).

steps.text: Clean the wick by burning it dry when the flame gets low, flickers, the knob gets stiff or tar builds on the wick: let the tank run out with the wick fully up, outside the living space and out of the wind, preferably in a sheltered spot outdoors; Toyotomi also names a well-ventilated garage (Toyotomi KS-27A, Toyotomi dry burn), where the big door should stay open because a garage is not 'outside' for CO (safety_carbon_monoxide). When it is cold, brush loose ash off the wick top gently and scrape tar off the wick adjuster.

Replace the wick when dry burning no longer brings the flame back, or the wick top is torn or burned down. Use the wick made for that model, check it moves smoothly and sits at the maker's height, and test the automatic shut-off before use (Toyotomi KS-27A).
steps.warn: Toyotomi says not to use the heater if the wick does not move smoothly and easily, or if its height at the top position is outside 7 to 9 mm (Toyotomi KS-27A).

steps.text: If the flame stays low after cleaning, suspect water. Drain the tank completely, dry it, fit a new wick and refill with fresh, clean kerosene (Toyotomi KS-27A).

At the end of the season, burn it dry, take out the last of the fuel with a syringe, and store it covered in a dry place (Toyotomi KS-27A). Keep kerosene outside the living space, away from petrol cans (CPSC 5052, Toyotomi KS-27A).

notes:
## What you are running
A kerosene wick heater has no chimney. Everything it burns goes into the room. Wick heaters sold as indoor heaters are certified for that: CSA B140.9.3 in Canada (portable kerosene heaters up to 4,400 W, 1-K kerosene only) and UL 647 in the US (CSA B140.9.3, UL 647). There are two kinds, convection and radiant (MSU E-1669); the KS-27A below has a reflector (Toyotomi KS-27A).

The Toyotomi KS-27A, a small model with a reflector, puts out about 2.9 kW (9,800 Btu/h) and burns about 21 hours on a 5.9 L tank; the larger Omni 230 is rated 23,000 Btu/h (6.7 kW) with a 7.5 L tank (Toyotomi KS-27A, Toyotomi Omni 230). Check the label for an altitude limit too: the Omni 230 is designed for use up to 1,300 m (Toyotomi Omni 230). See [reading heater labels](#guides/reference_heater_labels) before you trust any found heater indoors. Health Canada says to use kerosene, propane or oil space heaters in enclosed areas only if they are specifically designed for indoor use (Health Canada CO). MSU notes that some communities and states ban or restrict these heaters in homes (MSU E-1669), so check local rules where you can.

## Fuel
- **1-K only.** 1-K kerosene is low in sulphur; 2-K has much more sulphur and makes far more sulphur dioxide (MSU E-1669). Grades look the same, so 'water-clear' on its own does not prove 1-K (CPSC 5052, MSU E-1669).
- **Never petrol.** Even small amounts of petrol or solvent in kerosene greatly raise the risk of fire or explosion (CPSC 5052). The MSU bulletin adds that diesel and jet fuel may be just as dangerous in these heaters (MSU E-1669). Toyotomi's list of fuels never to use also names alcohol, white gas and camp-stove fuel (Toyotomi KS-27A).
- **Cans:** kerosene cans are usually blue and petrol cans red; never put kerosene in a can that held petrol (CPSC 5052). Toyotomi says a non-red can marked KEROSENE, never glass (Toyotomi KS-27A). Grabbing the petrol can by mistake is a major cause of heater fires (Toyotomi KS-27A).
- **Age:** Toyotomi says not to keep heater kerosene longer than 6 months and to start each season with fresh fuel. Old or poor fuel gives a low flame, tar on the wick, smoke, smell, a short wick life and trouble lighting or putting the heater out (Toyotomi KS-27A).
- **Checking found fuel:** pour a sample into a clear jar and let it settle. Toyotomi wants crystal-clear, colourless kerosene free of water and cloudiness, and says never to use yellow or sour-smelling fuel (Toyotomi KS-27A). A clear jar shows water and haze, not what the fuel is: different grades look the same (CPSC 5052, MSU E-1669). If you cannot say where the fuel came from, or it sat in a can that ever held petrol or solvent, do not burn it in the heater (CPSC 5052, Toyotomi KS-27A). See [fuel handling](#guides/safety_fuel_handling) for moving fuel safely.

## Air, CO and the room
Even a well-run heater gives off low levels of carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide, and these can harm people with heart or lung problems (CPSC 5052). Sulphur dioxide comes too (MSU E-1669). The rules (CPSC 5052, Toyotomi KS-27A):
- Door open to the rest of the house.
- An outside window open about 2.5 cm (1 in) if the door must be closed or the house is tight.
- Toyotomi's rule of thumb: a room needs at least 5.7 m³ (200 ft³) of air for every 1,000 Btu/h of heater, or the door or a window has to be open.

| Heater size | Room volume below which Toyotomi says keep the door open or open a window |
|---|---|
| 9,800 Btu/h (2.9 kW) | about 56 m³ (2,000 ft³), e.g. 5 × 4.5 m with a 2.5 m ceiling |
| 23,000 Btu/h (6.7 kW), e.g. Toyotomi Omni 230 | about 131 m³ (4,600 ft³) |

Worked from Toyotomi's 5.7 m³ per 1,000 Btu/h. In a room smaller than this, keep the door to the rest of the house open or open a window (Toyotomi KS-27A, Toyotomi Omni 230). A bigger room is not a licence to shut the door: Toyotomi's rule assumes a house of typical, not tight, construction, and CPSC says to run the heater with the room door open, plus a window open about 2.5 cm (1 in) in a tight or winterized house (Toyotomi KS-27A, CPSC 5052).

The heater is not something to sleep beside: turn it off before bed (Toyotomi KS-27A). Fit a CO alarm and know what it can't tell you: see [running heaters without CO poisoning](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide) and [carbon monoxide](#browse/hazards/co_gas).

## Flame and wick height
| What you see | Meaning (Toyotomi KS-27A) |
|---|---|
| Chamber glowing evenly red | Right |
| Smoke, soot, tall flame | Wick too high, chamber not seated, draught, or bad fuel |
| Smell, low flame | Wick too low or dirty, or bad fuel |
| Flame rising on its own | Room above about 30 °C (86 °F), or petrol in the fuel |

If the flame climbs and will not stay down, shut the heater off at once and treat the fuel as contaminated (Toyotomi KS-27A).

## Cleaning: burning dry
A dirty wick is the usual cause of a low, flickering, smelly flame. Toyotomi's method: loosen hard tar with pliers first, then let the heater burn its tank empty with the wick fully up, outside the living space and out of the wind (Toyotomi names a garage or a sheltered spot outdoors; keep a garage's big door open). Leave the dial up and let it go out by itself: turning it off early leaves the job half done. Fuel left in the tank only makes it take longer, so drain most of it first if you are short of time (Toyotomi dry burn). Once it is cold, brush the top of the wick gently with an old toothbrush, vacuum soot from around it, and scrape tar from the top of the wick adjuster and air tube (Toyotomi KS-27A).

## Replacing a wick
Use the wick made for that heater's model; Toyotomi warns that substitute wicks can seriously reduce performance and safety (Toyotomi KS-27A). Read the model number off the label before you go looking, and take the old wick to compare. On the KS-27A the wick hangs on three pins in a sleeve under three wing nuts; afterwards it must move freely and stand 7 to 9 mm high at the top position, and the automatic extinguisher must be tested again (Toyotomi KS-27A). Other models differ: follow their own figures. Trim loose threads on the top edge only; never cut the wick body (Toyotomi KS-27A).

## Troubleshooting
| Problem | Likely cause (Toyotomi KS-27A) |
|---|---|
| Will not light | Out of fuel, water in the fuel, poor fuel |
| Smoke or smell | Chamber not seated, wick too high, dirty wick, draught, bad fuel |
| Flickering, dying or low flame | Dirty wick, water in the fuel, wick burned too short |
| Stiff wick knob | Dirty wick, poor fuel |
| Flame too high | Petrol or other volatile fuel in the tank: shut it off at once, drain and rinse the tank, fit a new wick |

## Fire
A flaring heater: do not move it, use the shut-off, and leave if that fails (CPSC 5052). No water on it (Toyotomi KS-27A). Keep a smoke alarm on every level, outside sleeping areas and in bedrooms (CPSC 5052), and keep the way out of every sleeping room clear. More on house fires: [open flames and house fires](#browse/hazards/open_flame).
